lesson.title: Why Water Striders Don't Sink
lesson.summary: Surface tension is the extra energy needed to stretch or break a liquid's surface, and it arises because molecules at the surface are pulled inward by neighbors on only one side, an effect that is unusually strong in water because of hydrogen bonding.
lesson.body:
Surface tension is the resistance of a liquid's surface to being stretched or broken, and it is a direct consequence of the cohesive intermolecular forces acting between the liquid's own molecules. Inside the bulk of a liquid, a molecule is surrounded by neighboring molecules on all sides, so the attractive forces it experiences are pulled roughly equally in every direction and largely cancel out. A molecule sitting right at the surface, however, has neighboring liquid molecules beside it and below it, but no liquid molecules above it, only air. This lack of neighbors above means the net attractive force on a surface molecule pulls inward and sideways, toward the bulk of the liquid, rather than canceling out in all directions. The result is that the surface behaves somewhat like a stretched elastic membrane, resisting anything that would increase the surface area, since increasing surface area means pulling more molecules up into that unbalanced, lower-energy-unfavorable surface layer.

Because surface tension comes directly from the strength of a liquid's own cohesive intermolecular forces, liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have higher surface tension, following exactly the same reasoning used to compare liquids generally. Water has an unusually high surface tension compared to most other common liquids, and the explanation is the same hydrogen bonding network responsible for water's high boiling point: each water molecule can potentially form up to four hydrogen bonds with its neighbors, through its two O-H bonds as a donor and its two oxygen lone pairs as an acceptor, which is an unusually large number of strong attractive connections for a small molecule to have. That extensive hydrogen bonding pulls surface water molecules inward with far more force than the weaker dispersion or dipole-dipole forces present in most other liquids.

Water striders, the insects that appear to walk on the surface of ponds, are the clearest everyday demonstration of this effect. A water strider's weight is spread across its long, thin legs, which are also coated with tiny water-repelling hairs, so the pressure it exerts on the water's surface is not enough to break through the hydrogen-bonded surface layer. The insect's legs create small dimples in the surface, visibly deforming the elastic-like surface without piercing it, and the surface tension supports the insect's weight the same way a trampoline surface supports a person without tearing.

Surface tension also explains the shape of a meniscus, the curved surface a liquid forms inside a narrow container, though the direction of the curve depends on a comparison between cohesive forces (liquid molecules attracting each other) and adhesive forces (liquid molecules attracting the container's surface). Where those adhesive forces to the container are stronger than the liquid's own cohesion, as with water in a glass tube, the liquid climbs slightly up the container walls, producing a concave meniscus. This interplay between cohesion and adhesion, driven by the same surface tension discussed here and the same hydrogen bonding responsible for water's unusually strong cohesive forces, is also exactly what drives capillary action, the rise of liquid through a narrow tube against gravity.
